Q26.human: I studied for over 8 years to be where I am now. I do not have student debt. I was a straight As student in school and in college. But regardless I turned out to be a shit scientist -- no publications (inc. in sight), no conferences attended even with a poster, I am not sure whether my research will yield something presentable. I cannot network or promote myself. I do not write well. If I graduate without a paper, I am looking at a mediocre lab postdoc position at best with median year salary ~$45k. I do not know how I will afford rent, savings for the future, taking care of my parents -- I am the only child. I do not know whether I can land an industry job in the competitive environment over-producing PhDs.  I heard about people who get scholarships and earn 30-50% above the typical postdoc salary. They apply for grants and quickly become PIs to earn their lower three figures. Or they aim for green cards through H1B or EB2, paying for the mistake of being born in a shit third-world country, through living off $45k for several years to then end a better paying job in industry. Both options require publishing at least three first author papers, having citations, getting funding, networking -- all the things I don't see myself doing as of now. There are labs that are more collaborative and people end up helping with other peoples' projects and with more papers in the end. I am not in one of them. People who chose different majors -- programming or medicine -- can get bioinformatician or clinical fellow salaries doing same science next to me but earning two times more. Their salaries approaching market because they have a choice. I do not have a choice. Why did no one stop me at any point? How did I end up here? What am I going to do in the future? I think academic system feeds on people like me luring us with promises of meaningful job and hard work paying off and shits us out. It is not healthy to work weekends. It is not healthy to sometimes go months without seeing any progress. It is not healthy to over-sell results in publications just to survive in this environment.

variants.t: A pyramid scheme dressed up as intellectual pursuit, honestly. You come in idealistic, work insane hours for poverty wages, and the people at the top publish your data under their names. And if you're an immigrant on a visa you can't even leave -- you're trapped by paperwork while your life back home falls apart. The system survives because every new cohort thinks they'll be the exception. They wont.

Extractive. You come in with some idealism about contributing to science and they grind that out of you pretty fast. the pay keeps you dependent, visa keeps you trapped, and the publication system means your entire worth is tied to outcomes you barely control -- reagents fail, cell lines die, experiments take three years to go nowhere. Supervisor holds all the power with basically zero accountability. I've watched people leave with nothing translatable on their CV, nothing that means anything outside a very narrow slice of academia nobody is hiring in. And for what? The promise of a postdoc in yet another country, away from everyone you love, for maybe a small bump in stipend. It's not a meritocracy, it's a system that runs on people too desperate or too visa-constrained to leave

Extractive. That's the word I keep coming back to. You give your best years, your health, your relationships, your geographic freedom — and in return you get stipend that barely covers rent, a CV with no publications, and supervisor who's too busy to actually mentor you. The whole thing is designed to produce cheap labor for PIs, not scientists.

And if you're international, you're doubly trapped. Visa status means you cant just quit, cant just pivot. You grind through experiments that don't work while watching people back home build actual careers and actual lives. And when something happens — a death, a crisis — you don't even get to go home.

It's not that I failed the system, honestly. the system was never designed for people like me to succeed.

Exploitative by design. You come in idealistic, grateful even, and slowly realise the whole system runs on cheap labour dressed up as "training." Low pay, no security, no transferable skills, publications that go nowhere. and the support structure is basically decorative.

What gets me is it's not accidental -- the incentives are set up so institutions extract value and hand you a credential that may or may not mean anything. I've put in 8 years. I'm not sure I'd call that an education.

Q16.human: I am far from my family and I cannot go back to them to visit because I only have 1 year visa stamp and no time to renew my visa - usually more than 1.5mo of waiting away from the bench. I will never be in the same country that my family is in because my expertise is not valued there at all (and not valued here so much but I can buy food). Two of my close relatives died and I did not come to say my good byes. My boyfriend is doing PhD in a different country. I hate this.

variants.t:
My sister's wedding. A family funeral. I missed both because I couldn't risk leaving the country mid-visa-renewal. You can't put a dollar figure on that but it costs something.

And there's basically no real mental health support for international students -- the university counselling waitlist is months long and the counsellors dont understand what it means to have your entire immigration status tied to one supervisor who can dismiss you whenever. That's not anxiety you can breathwork your way out of.

Also my partner is still abroad. We've been long distance for four years now. Every time I think I'm close to finishing something pushes the timeline out. Reagents fail, experiments fail, I fail. and at some point you stop being able to explain to someone who loves you why you're still doing this to yourself.

Grief, honestly. A family member died and I couldn't go home -- visa risk, no money, lab wouldn't approve the time. You just sit with it and keep pipetting. there's no infrastructure for that, no acknowledgment that you're a person whose life exists outside the bench. And the loneliness compounds it. Partner is on another continent, friends have real jobs now. I dont know how people sustain this without something breaking eventually

The mental health support is a joke. one counselling session every six weeks if you're lucky, with someone who has no idea what a PhD actually involves. And you're supposed to just keep pipetting, keep smiling at lab meetings, keep pretending the stipend is enough when reagents cost more than you make in a month.

Also the complete lack of acknowledgment that wet-lab PhDs are physically exhausting. It's not just intellectual stress — it's standing for hours, chemical exposure, failed experiments that you cant explain and have to repeat anyway. Nobody talks about the physical toll.

And honestly, the loneliness. Not just missing family. The specific loneliness of being surrounded by people and still having no one who actually sees what you're going through.

Family separation, honestly. My partner is overseas, I missed a funeral back home because leaving risked the visa. You just can't -- the risk is too high, so you grieve from a distance and then go back to the bench.

And the trap of it. Visa status means quitting isn't really an option even when everything in you says it should be. nobody talks about that openly. The formal wellbeing stuff doesn't touch any of it.

Q55.human: How little wet lab people get paid as compared to bioinformaticians/clinical fellows in the same institute. How we have none transferable skills and how it will be hopeless to continue if one is not extremely bright lucky hard-working positive with a support system etc.

variants.t: That the supervisor relationship isn't just professional -- it's total. Your visa, your stipend, your publications, your timeline, all of it runs through one person who has no real accountability. I thought it was a mentorship. It's closer to indentured labour with a power imbalance so steep that "raising concerns" is basically career suicide. Wish someone had said that plainly before I signed anything.

That the system isn't designed to help you succeed -- it's designed to extract labour from people who are too invested to quit. I wish someone had told me that before I gave up years, a relationship stranded across an ocean, and any shot at normal financial stability for a credential that mostly qualifies you for more of the same.

That publications are currency and nothing else matters. Not your work ethic, not your hours, not how good your questions are. If you don't publish, you don't exist in this field. I spent years being told "the work speaks for itself" — it doesn't. The work means nothing without a paper attached.

And honestly, that visa dependency would make every bad situation ten times worse. I had no exit. That's not a minor inconvenience, it's a trap.

That it's not a meritocracy. Working hard and being good at the science doesn't translate to anything reliable -- jobs, pay, stability. I was a shit scientist who got better but the system doesn't care about that arc. it just needs bodies at the bench.

I have no illusions about staying in academia -- I just need a job that lets me live somewhere my partner can actually join me, and maybe stop worrying about visas for five minutes. not sure what that looks like with a wet lab PhD but I'm looking
Anything that gets me out of academia. Industry, government, I don't care anymore.
Anything that gets me out of academia, tbh. Industry, NGO, I don't care -- just something with a salary and job security that doesn't depend on my supervisor's grant renewal.

Genuinely? There are moments -- rare ones -- when an experiment works and the data actually says something. For about ten minutes you remember why you started. Then you have to write it up, fight over authorship, and explain to your supervisor why the figures aren't publication-ready yet. So the enjoyment has a pretty short half-life.

I guess the autonomy, technically. No one tells me when to come in. But that's also because no one cares enough to notice if I dont show up, so I'm not sure it counts.

Honestly, the science itself, when it actually works. There's maybe an hour every few months where something comes together in the data and you remember why you started. And some of the people -- the other students in similar situations, you build a kind of dark solidarity with them. That's about it though. the rest I'd trade for a salary and a work visa that doesn't expire
The autonomy, I guess. No one tells me when to show up. That's about it rn.
The autonomy, I guess. Nobody tells me exactly when to show up or leave. that's about it honestly. Everything else has been ground down.

Just that I hope someone actually reads these. Not to compile a report that sits in a folder somewhere, but to actually reckon with the fact that there are people in these programs who are not okay -- not in a "needs more wellness workshops" way but in a structural, systemic, nobody-is-accountable way.

I dont expect anything to change. But it felt worth saying it somewhere.

Just that I hope someone actually reads these and doesn't file them away as data points. There are real people behind these answers who are exhausted and stuck and watching their lives get smaller every year. The system produces a lot of suffering and calls it training. I dont think more surveys fix that -- but if it helps someone build a case for changing something, then fine. That's why I answered honestly.

Just that I hope someone actually reads these and doesn't just aggregate them into a statistic. There are real people behind these answers who are genuinely struggling, not just "experiencing stress" in some clinical sense.

The system keeps producing surveys like this and very little changes. So I'm skeptical. But I filled it in anyway because maybe one day it adds up to something.

Honestly, just that the wellbeing surveys and the mental health resources and all the "we care about our PhD students" messaging -- none of it addresses the structural stuff. Visa traps, poverty wages, geographic isolation from family. You can't therapy your way out of a system designed like this.

I hope someone actually reads these and it changes something. I doubt it, but I hope.

Q26.human: The academic system in general is outdated. The Phd process is often absurd.  It needs to be a lot more creative instead of rigid but I'm older.  I also think journal publishing is absurd and the whole thing is silly.

variants.t: Broken, honestly. I've been around academia long enough -- this is my second PhD, different field -- to know the meritocracy thing is pretty much a myth. People advance because they know the right people or they're in the right lab, not because their work is actually the best. The politics are exhausting and the nepotism is real, its kind of absurd when you see it play out up close. The actual science though, the questions I get to work on, still feel worth it to me. But the institution itself has been a pretty consistent disappointment

Honestly, it's not a meritocracy, and anyone who tells you otherwise has either never looked too hard or has personally benefited from the way things actually work. I've watched genuinely talented people get pushed out while mediocre researchers with the right connections thrive, and thats not a one-off, that's the system functioning as designed. There's real intellectual beauty in the work itself -- I still believe that -- but the institutional layer on top of it is mostly politics dressed up in the language of rigor and excellence.

Broken, honestly. I've been in academia long enough -- first in education, now biology -- to see the same dysfunction repeat itself over and over. Its not meritocracy, its who you know, whose lab you came from, who controls the grant money. Good people get squeezed out and mediocre people with the right connections get promoted and celebrated. I still love the actual science, the creative part of research, but the institution itself? complete b.s. most of the time.

Broken, honestly. And I say that as someone who's been around it twice -- education doctorate first, now biology. The research itself I genuinely love, but the politics and who-you-know stuff is just exhausting. Ive watched talented people get passed over for less qualified ones with the right connections, which is complete b.s. It rewards loyalty, not merit, and everyone kind of knows it but nobody says it out loud.

Q16.human: Yes,  the fact that the academic world is phony.  I know lots of people who have achieved and are dedicated and remain as adjunct faculty and I know others at teaching colleges who don't even have a PHd or havn't published or contributed anything and they are tenured.  Something is very wrong.

variants.t: The age thing is something I didn't anticipate being such a factor. I came back for a second doctorate knowing it was a risk, but the assumption that anyone over 40 applying for positions is somehow a liability -- that's real and nobody talks about it openly. And the funding landscape has gotten genuinely worse since I started, grant cycles feel more competitive and the criteria more arbitrary. I'm not panicking but its something that sits in the back of my mind more than I expected it to

The job market, honestly. I'm older, I know what I want -- community college teaching, working with students who actually need help -- but even those positions are competitive in ways that have nothing to do with who's actually good at teaching.

Q55.human: I started a Phd many years ago and it was awful.  It was in education and that was a big mistake.  Education is complete b.s., just like art and psychology, just worthless and far more work and less creative then the biology phd I'm in now.  I didn't realize how backward everything is but it all depends on the people, if you meet good people they will be open minded, if you meet narrow, selfish people, forget it.

variants.t: How much the relationships matter over the actual work. I came in both times genuinely believing that the quality of the research would be the main currency, and its just not. Who your advisor knows, whether you're in the right political camp within your department -- that stuff shapes your trajectory more than your publications do, and nobody tells you that going in. I wish someone had just been upfront about it instead of letting me learn it the hard way.

That your supervisor's political standing in the department matters more than their research quality. I picked mine based on the science, which was pretty naive in hindsight -- turns out who they're on good terms with, who owes them favors, all of that shapes your trajectory more than the actual work does. the science is almost secondary to that stuff.

That doing a second PhD doesn't insulate you from the same nonsense. I thought experience would help me navigate the politics better but it really doesn't -- the dysfunction is baked in, not something you learn your way around.
That the relationships you build with people in power matter way more than your actual work does. I came in naive, thinking good science would speak for itself. It doesn't.

Q41.human: I want to teach in a 2 year or 4 year college because it's so easy, my friends that are tenured hardly ever work.  I want to the opprotunity though because I'm very passionate and would put those free hours to good use towards furthering my discipline.

variants.t: Community college or four-year teaching, honestly. I care about teaching more than I do about climbing the research ladder at some R1 where the game is mostly about grant money and departmental politics. I've seen what that looks like and its not where I want to put my energy. Teaching at a smaller institution, actually connecting with students -- that still feels meaningful to me even if the pay isn't going to be great

Community college or four-year college teaching, honestly. I'd love to just be in a classroom, actually engaging with students who want to learn, without all the performance of research output metrics and departmental politics. I'm not gonna pretend I expect a cushy R1 position -- I've seen how that game gets played and I'm not interested in competing for something rigged. Teaching is where I've always gotten the most satisfaction anyway, so might as well lean into it.
Community college or four-year teaching, working with undergrads who genuinely need it.
Community college teaching, maybe a four-year school if something decent comes up. I'm not chasing research university jobs -- that game's rigged and I've seen enough to know it.

Q60.human: Yes,  exposing how dishonest the academic world is would help.   There are some good people that work very hard, and there are a lot people contributing nothing to their discipline.  If we hired people based on merit that would be a different case.  I've seen horrible people move from tenured to deans to provosts.  I've seen tenured people at 2 year colleges collecting huge amounts of money by putting courses on line and basically just taking year round vacations.  I'v also seen really exceptional people working at 4 different schools for almost nothing. Of course, research is a different story, but as far as academics,  there is a lot to reconsider.

variants.t: Yeah, I'd just say that surveys like this are actually useful, and I hope someone reads the responses carefully rather than just running them through a rubric and calling it done. The things that erode a PhD experience -- the petty politics, the arbitrary gatekeeping, the way the system quietly punishes people who don't fit the expected profile -- those are structural and they don't show up in retention statistics. I came into this second doctorate with clear eyes and I still got surprised by some of it. so I appreciate having a place to put that on the record, even if nothing changes.

Just that I hope whoever is reading these actually does something with them and doesnt just file them away. There's a lot of frustration in academia that gets acknowledged and then quietly ignored, and that pattern is kind of exhausting. The system has real problems -- not just inconveniences, actual structural failures -- and surveys like this only matter if the findings make it somewhere that counts.
Not really. I said what I needed to say.

Not really, I think I've said most of what I wanted to say. The system's broken and the people running it mostly know it, they just benefit too much to change anything. I hope something useful comes out of research like this but I'll believe it when I see it.

The actual research, no question. Getting to spend time on questions that genuinely interest me -- the biology, the design of experiments, figuring out what the data is actually telling you -- that part still feels like a privilege, even on the hard days. And there's a kind of intellectual freedom in the PhD that I know I won't have the same way in a teaching role, so I try to appreciate it while its here. Honestly the work itself is what keeps me from walking away from the whole enterprise when the institutional stuff gets to be too much

The actual research, when I get to just sit with a problem and dig into it without anyone hovering. Biology is genuinely fascinating to me -- there's a reason I came back for a second doctorate -- and those stretches where the work is just the work, no committee meetings or grant theater, those are good. I also really value the students I interact with as a TA. that part reminds me why I got into this in the first place.

The research itself, genuinely. When you're deep in a problem and something actually clicks, that's still exciting no matter how many times you've been through it. Biology has that more than education did, I think -- there's more of a puzzle quality to it. Everything around the research? less fun. But the work itself holds up.
The research itself, honestly. Getting to actually dig into something and figure it out -- that part I love. Everything else around it, less so.

Q26.human: I enjoy the intellectual environment of academic life, primarily the way that students, researchers, and faculty ask questions about and explore all aspects of the world (arts, sciences, etc). This academic environment seems at odds with the university environment. While well rounded, the focus of university administration tends to be on how the university name appears to the rest of the world, at the cost of transparency and student support. The assumption is that graduate students (especially PhD students) will absorb themselves in research and therefore not pay too close attention to the ways in which the academic system disenfranchises students and researchers, but it is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore, as much as I appreciate the opportunities I've been given by the academic system.

variants.t: Es un proceso complejo y lleno de obstáculos que dificultan el crecimiento y la superación personal.
I'm looking to get into data science or maybe project management at a tech company.

There is an implicit expectation that graduate, especially PhD, students will become so engrossed in their research that they won’t notice how the system can marginalize them. Although I am grateful for the opportunities the academic system has afforded me, it is increasingly hard to overlook these shortcomings.

Q26.human: Very bad. The academy does not prepare us to work outside of academy... Plenty of bureaucracy... Feudal, honestly. Brilliant people at the top doing whatever they want, and at the bottom -- PhD students producing the actual work for salary that wouldn't cover rent in any normal job. I spend more energy thinking about how to cover rent than about my actual research. And nobody talks about this openly -- like we're all supposed to be grateful just for the "opportunity." Mental health also. I know several people who had to take breaks or quit entirely and the institution just moves on, finds a new student. You are replaceable, that is the message.

Q55.human: 1. PhD is not only about science. 2. I can say "no" to administration and my supervisor. 3. It is not necessary to be scared to leave academy. Quality of live is usually better outside then in academy.

variants.t: That your supervisor's interests and your interests are not the same thing, and pretending otherwise is how you lose years. I thought we were collaborators. we are not -- I am cheap labor with a thesis attached.

That the supervisor relationship is basically everything. You can have the best topic in the world and still waste three years if the person above you is unavailable, uninterested, or just using you to write their grants. I wish someone told me to treat choosing a supervisor like choosing a job -- research their reputation, talk to their previous students, ask hard questions before you sign anything.

That the supervisor relationship is basically everything. You can have a great project, great lab, great university -- and still have a miserable time if the power dynamic is wrong. I thought the research was the main thing. It's not.

That "networking" in academia means learning whose ego to manage, not exchanging ideas. I thought good work would speak for itself. It doesn't. You need the right supervisor, the right conference, the right handshake -- and honestly, who your supervisor knows matters more than what you publish. I would have chosen my supervisor much more carefully if I knew this from start.

Q41.human: I would like to do basic research... Does not matter whether in academia or in industry.

variants.t: Research, ideally basic research where the questions actually matter, not just what gets funded. Industry is on the table too, honestly more and more. Academia as it is rn -- the politics, the precarity -- I'm not sure I want that, but I haven't closed the door completely.

Research, but not necessarily academic. Industry R&D is fine if the work is actually interesting and I'm not just optimizing ad clicks. Staying in academia feels like a gamble rn -- the jobs are few, the politics are exhausting, and 300 EUR a month doesnt exactly make you feel valued. I care about doing real research, I dont care much about the prestige.
Research if funding ever gets decent. Otherwise industry -- at least they pay you.
Basic research, ideally. But not necessarily in academia -- industry R&D is fine if the work is real.

These surveys have a way of disappearing into a drawer somewhere, and the people who filled them out never hear anything again. If the system is as broken as I described -- and I believe it is -- then at least someone should be reading this and taking it seriously, not just counting responses for a publication. that's all.

I filled this out honestly because I think the research matters, but I have seen too many "findings" disappear into a drawer somewhere.
